title: The Signal
author: Alexandre Dias
contentWarnings: Themes of loneliness and being chosen
excerpt: The signal came in at 1420.406 MHz. It came in on the seventh night of Isabela Rocha's shift at the ATCA, during a routine observation of NGC 5253. It sounded, at first, like a small dry cough. On the third occurrence, she understood it was a word. It was in no human language. It was, unmistakably, being said.

chapters.title: Hertz
chapters.body:
The signal came in at 1420.406 MHz.

It came in on the seventh night of Isabela Rocha's shift at the ATCA — the Australia Telescope Compact Array, six twenty-two-meter dishes arrayed on a six-kilometer rail in the flat scrubland of central New South Wales, where she had come as a postdoctoral fellow of the Anglo-Australian Observatory to spend eighteen months on a survey of hydrogen emission from nearby dwarf galaxies. She had, that night, been the sole astronomer on shift. She had been on shift for the past six hours. She had been drinking, as she always drank on the long overnight shifts, weak black tea from the small canteen down the corridor from the control room, and she had been listening — because the ATCA processed its data into audio streams as well as into visual displays, and because she had, since her doctoral work, found it easier to detect certain kinds of anomaly by ear than by eye — to the small quiet hiss of the hydrogen line as the array integrated the signal from the current target.

The target had been NGC 5253. It was a small starburst galaxy, thirteen million light-years distant. It had been observed many times before. Its hydrogen emission had been characterized, at the resolution of the ATCA, more than adequately for the purposes of Isabela's survey, and she had, that night, been running the observation partly as a calibration check and partly, in the honest truth of it, because she liked the way NGC 5253 looked at the eyepiece of the small refractor she kept on the roof of the control building. It had, over the last three months, become her favorite galaxy. Astronomers were not, in general, supposed to have favorite galaxies. She had, in the specific quiet privacy of her long night shifts, allowed herself to have one.

The hydrogen line had been coming in as a small smooth hiss.

At 2:47 in the morning, the hiss had, briefly, been interrupted.

It had been interrupted by something that had sounded, when she had first heard it in her headphones, like a small dry cough.

She had, in the moment, thought it was interference. She had reached forward and had, without particular urgency, checked the RFI monitor. The RFI monitor had shown no interference. She had checked the receiver diagnostics. The receiver diagnostics had shown nominal operation. She had, in the way of a tired astronomer at three in the morning, been about to note the anomaly in the shift log and to move on.

Then she had heard the cough again.

It had been, this time, a little louder. It had, also, sounded — she had noticed this with the specific late-shift attention that was different from ordinary attention — it had sounded a little more *shaped*. It had not been a cough exactly. It had been more like a small dry syllable. A vowel and a consonant. It had had, in the small compressed way of a very short sound, a *character*.

She had reached forward. She had adjusted the audio filtering. She had increased the gain on the specific narrow band around the hydrogen line. She had waited.

The sound had come a third time.

This time she had, quite clearly, heard it.

It had been, unmistakably, a word.

It had been a single short word, in a language she could not identify — one syllable, roughly the length of the English word *stop*, spoken in the small quiet way of someone speaking into a private device rather than into a room. She had not been able to distinguish the phonemes with any confidence. It had been too brief. But it had been, in the whole of its shape, a word.

She had sat still in her chair.

She had listened.

She had listened for perhaps ten minutes. Nothing further had come. The hydrogen line had settled back into its ordinary hiss. The receiver diagnostics had continued to report nominal. The RFI monitor had continued to show no interference. The observation had continued.

She had reached forward. She had, quite quietly, saved the last twenty minutes of raw audio data to her personal drive. She had labeled the file *NGC5253_247_anomaly.wav.*

She had, after some consideration, not entered the anomaly in the shift log.

She had, after further consideration, entered the shift log at 3:00 exactly, and had described the last six hours of observation as *nominal, no events of interest.*

She had not, at the time she had done this, been able to say why. She had thought about it, briefly, and had told herself that she wanted to review the audio in daylight before deciding whether it warranted a log entry. This had been, at the time, a plausible justification. She had believed it, more or less, for perhaps four minutes.

Then she had, in the specific honest way she had learned to be honest with herself over the years of her PhD, admitted that she had, at some level below thinking, decided that the audio was hers. That she was not going to share it. That she was going to sit with it, for at least a little while, before permitting anyone else to hear it.

She had, in her small quiet way, understood that this was not what she was supposed to do.

She had gone on doing it.

—

She had listened to the file the following afternoon.

She had, after her shift, driven the forty minutes back to her small rented cottage in Narrabri, and had slept for six hours, and had woken at eleven, and had, over her second cup of coffee, opened the file on her personal laptop with headphones on.

The file had been twenty minutes long.

The anomalies had begun at the fourteen-minute mark. The first had been the small dry cough she had first heard. It had been, on second listen, less clearly a cough than she had thought at the time — more like a small burst of shaped noise, a click and a hiss compressed into perhaps a fifth of a second. The second, twenty seconds later, had been longer and clearer. The third, forty seconds after that, had been the one that had made her sit still at the console.

She listened to the third anomaly seven times.

Each time she was more certain it was a word.

She could not, however, identify the word. She had tried, on the second and third listens, to write down what she was hearing — to render it in phonetic notation on the back of an envelope she had found in the kitchen — and had produced, over the several attempts, three different transcriptions. The first had been *kroh.* The second had been *khral.* The third had been *khan.* None of them had seemed, on subsequent listening, right.

The word was, she thought after her seventh listen, in a language whose phoneme set she did not know. It was not, so far as she could tell, in any Indo-European language, and not in any of the languages she had encountered in her work with international colleagues over the years — no Mandarin, no Japanese, no Arabic. It was not, she thought, any human language she had ever heard.

She had, at this thought, closed the laptop.

She had sat at her small kitchen table for a long moment.

She had opened the laptop.

She had listened again.

—

She had gone back on shift the following night.

She had, before going in, made a decision. She had decided that she was going to run the receiver on a small parallel process — a private one, a piggyback on the ordinary survey observations, that she would not enter into the main data log — that would sit on the hydrogen line and record continuously to her personal drive, throughout every shift she took, for the next several weeks. She was going to build up a catalog of what she was hearing. She was going to determine whether the anomaly repeated, and if so, at what rate, and whether it appeared in observations of other galaxies or only in observations of NGC 5253.

She had begun the parallel recording at seven that evening.

She had, on that night, on the observation of a different galaxy — the small dwarf irregular IC 4662 — heard nothing anomalous. The hydrogen line had come in as its ordinary hiss for the full six hours. The parallel recording had captured six hours of clean data.

She had, on the following night, observed NGC 5253 again for a two-hour block she had inserted into her schedule under a pretext of extra calibration.

She had heard the anomaly at 3:12.

It had been, this time, a single word. Longer than the one two nights earlier. Perhaps a full second of shaped sound. It had been, she thought when she played it back at her cottage the following afternoon, more clearly a word than any of the earlier fragments. She had, on this listen, been able to write down a somewhat more stable transcription: *khreh-lan.*

It had, she thought, been two syllables.

It had also, she thought, been said — she had no other word — *deliberately.* The earlier anomalies had had the character of a person clearing their throat, or muttering to themselves, or beginning to speak and stopping. This one had been said fully. It had been articulated. It had, in the small careful way of a spoken word, been *offered* into her headphones.

She had sat with the recording for a long time that afternoon.

She had, at the end of it, opened her personal notebook — a small green Moleskine she had been keeping since her PhD, into which she had, over the years, written the small honest observations she had not been willing to put into any professional log — and had, at the top of a fresh page, written the following:

*NGC 5253 hydrogen line audio anomalies. Second observation confirmed. Distinct syllabic structure. Not RFI. Not receiver artifact. Provisional transcription: KHREH-LAN. Not any language I recognize.*

She had, after a moment, added:

*I am not going to tell anyone yet.*

She had underlined the last sentence.

—

She had, over the following six weeks, recorded thirty-two additional anomalies.

They had appeared, without exception, only during observations of NGC 5253. She had confirmed this by systematically observing other galaxies for equivalent lengths of time and had detected nothing anomalous in any of them. The anomalies were specific to NGC 5253. They were, further, not evenly distributed in time — they came in what she had begun to think of as *bursts*, of two or three closely-spaced words within a ten-minute window, followed by long periods, sometimes hours, of nothing.

They were also getting longer.

The first anomaly, on the seventh night, had been a fifth of a second. The last anomaly of the six-week period — recorded on the forty-seventh night of her private survey — had been eleven seconds long. It had contained, so far as she could tell from her transcription, perhaps fourteen or fifteen syllables. It had been, unmistakably, a whole sentence.

She had, by the end of the six weeks, catalogued in her Moleskine perhaps eighty distinct words. She had not been able to identify any of them. She had cross-referenced her transcriptions against every language database she had been able to find. She had, over the course of one long weekend, taught herself the basics of the Semitic root system so as to check whether the words might be from an ancient language whose modern descendants had lost the phonemes. They had not been. She had checked against Basque, against the Ainu language, against Khoisan click languages. She had checked against reconstructed Proto-Indo-European. She had, on the last Saturday of the six-week period, spent an entire afternoon checking her transcriptions against samples of every language she could find in the university library that had fewer than a thousand living speakers.

Nothing had matched.

The words were, so far as she could determine, in no human language.

She had sat at her small kitchen table in her small cottage in Narrabri on that last Saturday evening, and she had drunk a large glass of white wine, and she had understood the following thing:

She had, in the whole of the six weeks, been hearing a person speak.

Not a signal. Not a pattern. Not a natural phenomenon of any kind. A person. A person with a voice, a language, a way of pronouncing syllables. A person who was, at 1420.406 MHz, coming through the ATCA's receivers as small compressed bursts of shaped sound during observations of a starburst galaxy thirteen million light-years away.

She had, for a moment, considered getting up and telephoning someone.

She had considered telephoning her old thesis supervisor in Cambridge. She had considered telephoning the director of the ATCA. She had considered telephoning her mother, in Recife, who was not an astronomer but who was the person in her life she trusted most.

She had, in the end, telephoned none of them.

She had, instead, poured a second glass of wine, and she had sat with the recording on her laptop, and she had listened, once more, to the sentence from the forty-seventh night.

She had listened to it, that evening, perhaps forty times.

She had, by the end of the evening, understood one thing about it. Not the meaning. She still did not know what any of the words meant. But she had understood, from the small internal rhythm of the sentence, the way its syllables rose and fell, the way it grouped its stresses:

It was a question.

Someone, thirteen million light-years away, was asking her a question.

She did not know what to answer.

chapters.title: The Response
chapters.body:
She began to answer on the sixty-second night.

She did this, at first, without meaning to. She had continued, throughout the eighth and ninth weeks of her private survey, to observe NGC 5253 during her regular shifts, and to record the anomalies as they came, and to catalog them in her Moleskine. She had, by then, catalogued a hundred and twelve distinct words in what she had begun, in her own private way, to think of as the language of the sixty-nine — because there had been sixty-nine recorded transmissions in the eight weeks she had been listening.

On the sixty-second night she had, during a long anomaly of nine seconds' duration, been alone in the control room. She had been, as always, listening with her headphones on. She had, in the specific small way of a woman who had been listening to the same voice speaking words she could not understand for weeks, said, aloud into the empty control room, quietly:

*I do not understand you.*

She had said it in Portuguese. It had been, in the small tired hour of five in the morning, the first language that had come to her mind. She had spoken quietly. She had not been thinking about being heard. She had, if anything, been talking to herself.

She had said it during the transmission, over the sound of the words coming through her headphones.

The transmission had, at the moment she had spoken, altered.

She had felt this, at first, as a kind of small hesitation in the sound. The rhythm of the words had, for perhaps a fraction of a second, faltered. And then the transmission had continued, but *differently* — the syllables had come more slowly, with longer pauses between them, in the specific way of a person who had, mid-sentence, been interrupted and had, after a moment, resumed at a more deliberate pace.

She had sat very still.

She had, after a moment, said again, aloud: *I do not understand you.*

The transmission had stopped.

There had been silence. The hydrogen line had settled to its ordinary hiss. The receiver diagnostics had continued to report nominal.

She had waited.

Ninety seconds had passed.

Then a new transmission had begun. It had been short — perhaps two seconds, four or five syllables. It had been in a rhythm and cadence she had not heard before. It had been, she understood as she listened to it, an *answer.*

She had said, aloud, again: *I still do not understand.*

She had said it in English this time.

The transmission had stopped.

A new one had begun. It had been perhaps three seconds, six or seven syllables. In a different rhythm again. She had listened, and had, at the end of it, sat in the small quiet of the control room, and had, very carefully, said aloud:

*Do you hear me.*

The transmission had begun immediately. It had been the longest since she had begun listening. It had gone on for perhaps fourteen seconds. It had contained, so far as she could count, twenty syllables. It had had, at its beginning, a specific short syllable that she had heard many times in the last eight weeks and had come, without deciding, to think of as *yes.*

She had, at the end of the transmission, put her hands flat on the console.

She had said, aloud, in Portuguese:

*Meu Deus.*

She had understood, at that moment, what she had been doing for eight weeks.

She had understood that she had been *communicating* with something. That she had not, as she had until that morning half-imagined, been listening to a broadcast — a signal being sent out from somewhere, without regard to who received it. She had, instead, been part of an exchange. She had been observing NGC 5253 for eight weeks, and during every observation she had been listening, and during every listening period the thing at the far end had been speaking, and it had been speaking because it had known, in some way she could not identify, that she was listening.

It had been listening back.

—

She had, over the following weeks, established several things.

She had established that the exchange was, in some sense, real-time. The other party responded to what she said — not always in a way she could understand, but always within about ninety seconds of her speaking. This was, in ordinary physics, impossible. NGC 5253 was thirteen million light-years away. A signal traveling at the speed of light would take thirteen million years to reach the galaxy and thirteen million more to return. Any real-time exchange between herself and something in NGC 5253 was, on the ordinary understanding of relativity, precluded.

Which meant that either NGC 5253 was not, in fact, where the signal was coming from — or the ordinary understanding did not apply.

She had, in her Moleskine, considered both possibilities and had noted her intention to think about neither of them in any detail for the moment.

She had established that the other party could, up to a point, learn. Over the following weeks, she had begun to introduce specific words in English into her spoken responses — *yes*, *no*, *hello*, *goodbye*, *stop*, *continue* — and had, over several weeks, begun to hear these same words come back through her headphones, in the small compressed shaped sound of the anomalies. The other party had been learning her language.

She had established, more disturbingly, that the other party could produce the words with a fidelity that was, to her ear, indistinguishable from her own pronunciation.

She had recorded her own voice saying *hello* on the ninety-third night. Two nights later, during an observation of NGC 5253, she had heard, coming through her headphones at 1420.406 MHz, a compressed shaped sound that had been, when she had played it back at her cottage the following afternoon, her own voice saying *hello.*

She had sat in her cottage for a long time.

She had understood, sitting in her cottage, that the exchange was not, whatever else it was, an exchange between two equal parties. She was, at her end, using ordinary radio astronomy equipment and her own voice speaking into an empty control room. She was doing, in other words, the small things a human astronomer could do. The other party was doing something else. The other party was, at whatever distance it actually was, capable of receiving her voice and reproducing it back to her within ninety seconds. It was capable of learning her language over a few weeks. It was capable of producing sounds in that language with what appeared to be perfect fidelity.

The exchange was not, in any ordinary sense, symmetric. She was the small careful ape at the eyepiece. The other party was — she permitted herself to think this, in her cottage, over a large glass of wine — the other party was something else.

She had continued to speak to it.

She had not, at any point in the fourteen weeks she had been listening, told anyone.

—

She had told Marcus on the hundred and second night.

Marcus was her partner. He was a mining engineer who had, over the last two years, been based in Sydney and had been visiting her at the cottage in Narrabri roughly one weekend a month. He was thirty-nine, unmarried, patient, uninterested in astronomy in any professional way but happy to listen when she talked about her work.

He had come up on a Friday evening. They had made dinner. They had sat, over red wine, in the small sitting room of the cottage.

She had said, at some point during the second glass: *Marcus.*

He had said: *yes.*

She had said: *I want to tell you something.*

She had told him.

She had told him carefully. She had told him from the seventh night. She had told him about the coughs and the words and the six-week catalog. She had told him about the sixty-second night and *I do not understand you* and the shift in the transmission. She had told him about the last weeks, and the exchange, and her voice being spoken back at her.

She had shown him the audio.

She had, when it was over, waited for him to speak.

He had, for a long moment, not spoken.

He had said, at last: *Isabela.*

She had said: *yes.*

He had said: *how long have you been alone with this.*

She had said: *fourteen weeks.*

He had said: *and you have not told anyone.*

She had said: *no.*

He had said: *not the director. Not your supervisor. Not — Isabela, this is — this is —*

She had said: *I know what it is.*

He had said: *it is the discovery of the century. Of the millennium. It is — my God, it is —*

She had said: *I know.*

He had looked at her.

He had said, more slowly: *and you have not told anyone.*

She had said, quietly: *no.*

He had put down his wine glass.

He had said: *Isabela. Why.*

She had thought about this question.

She had thought about it for perhaps a full minute. She had thought about the answers she had rehearsed, in her small kitchen at her small cottage over the last fourteen weeks. She had considered the answer that had to do with wanting to be sure, with wanting to rule out every possible mundane explanation, with wanting to protect a preliminary result from being taken up too early by an eager scientific community. She had considered the answer that had to do with career — with wanting to be, when the announcement came, the sole first author, the person whose name would appear in the encyclopedias.

Neither of those answers had been the true one.

She had said, at last:

*Because it has been speaking only to me.*

Marcus had looked at her.

She had said: *and I have been the one it has been speaking to. And I have not, in the whole of my life, been the one anyone has spoken to like this. And I did not want, in the first weeks, to give that up.*

She had said: *and now it has been fourteen weeks, and I have been in this conversation, and I have not been able, at any point in those fourteen weeks, to think of a moment at which I would have been willing to tell someone. I have not been able to think of a version of the announcement in which the conversation continues to be mine. So I have not made the announcement.*

She had said, more quietly: *I know how this sounds.*

Marcus had, for a very long moment, not spoken.

He had said, at last: *Isabela. This is not yours.*

She had said: *I know.*

He had said: *this is — this is a thing the whole of humanity should be part of. This is — this is not something one person can keep to themselves. This is not a diary entry. This is — this is contact.*

She had said: *I know.*

He had said: *you have to tell.*

She had said: *I know.*

He had said: *when.*

She had said: *soon.*

He had held her gaze.

He had said: *tomorrow.*

She had said: *not tomorrow.*

He had said: *Isabela.*

She had said: *not tomorrow.*

They had, that night, gone to bed without further speaking. Marcus had left the following morning earlier than he had planned. He had said, at the door, that he loved her, and that he would be back the following weekend, and that they would talk about it then. She had said yes.

She had known, when he had left, that he would not, in fact, be back the following weekend. He would call. He would say the small careful things a partner said when they had understood, quite suddenly, that they had, in the whole of a two-year relationship, misjudged the person they had been with. And they would agree, in the small tired way of two people who had loved each other and had discovered a small essential mismatch, that it was, perhaps, time to think about things.

She had known this. She had let him go.

She had gone back to the control room that evening. She had begun her shift. She had, at 3:14 in the morning, during an observation of NGC 5253, heard through her headphones a specific compressed shaped sound.

The sound had been her own voice.

The voice had said: *I know.*

She had understood, sitting at the console, that the other party had been listening the previous night — that it had heard, through some mechanism she did not understand, the conversation between her and Marcus in her sitting room in the cottage in Narrabri.

She had understood that it had been listening to her, in her home, in her private life, for some time.

She had, for a moment, been afraid.

She had, then, understood something else.

She had understood that if the other party had been listening for some time, it had had many opportunities to reveal itself, or to make its listening felt, and had not. It had been, quite deliberately, quiet. It had chosen, in its own way, to preserve for her the illusion that the exchange was limited to the control room. It had, in other words, been *considerate.*

The consideration had, in some way she could not immediately explain to herself, comforted her.

She had said, quietly, into the control room:

*You have been listening for a long time.*

The transmission had come after a pause.

The voice — her own voice — had said, in the specific quiet way she had come to associate with the other party's more considered responses:

*Yes.*

She had said: *how long.*

The transmission had come again.

Her own voice had said: *since the seventh night.*

She had sat with this.

She had said, at last: *why did you not tell me.*

The transmission had come.

Her own voice had said: *you were not ready.*

She had sat for a long moment.

She had said, quietly: *and now?*

The transmission had come. Her own voice, quiet and careful:

*Now you are.*

chapters.title: The Line
chapters.body:
She did not, in the end, tell anyone.

She thought about it for many weeks. She thought about it every day. She rehearsed, in the small quiet hours of her long shifts, the various shapes of the announcement she might make. She rehearsed calling her thesis supervisor in Cambridge. She rehearsed calling the director of the ATCA. She rehearsed writing the paper, drafting the press release, sitting in the small careful room where the interview would be held and answering the small careful questions the journalists would ask.

She could not, in any of these rehearsals, arrive at a version in which the announcement did not end the exchange.

She had thought about this at length. She had, in her Moleskine, made lists. She had considered every possibility. She had considered whether the other party might, in some way, continue to communicate with her privately even after a public announcement. She had considered whether she could, once the announcement was made, negotiate for some private channel to be preserved. She had considered whether the other party would, on its own initiative, refuse to speak to anyone else, and continue to speak only to her.

She had, over the weeks, understood that these were all fantasies. Once the announcement was made, the exchange would be taken from her. It would become a public matter. Other people would come to the ATCA. Other people would be at the console. Other observations would be made. The other party would, in some form, continue to communicate — but the communication would be a public thing, mediated by many hands, and Isabela Rocha would be, in the great arrangement of it, only one voice among many.

She had understood, further, that this was probably the correct outcome.

She had understood that she had, for whatever reasons, been the first to hear — that the choice of her as first receiver had been, in the small quiet way of a universe that made these choices without explanation, a matter of chance. She had happened to be at the console on the seventh night. She had happened to be listening on headphones. She had happened to have the specific small habit of noting anomalies before entering them in the log. Any of these had been contingent. Another astronomer, in her chair on the seventh night, would have been the first to hear. And that other astronomer, presumably, would have done the responsible thing and told someone.

She had, sitting in her cottage on a Tuesday evening in June, understood that she was not going to do the responsible thing.

She had understood this without particular guilt.

She had understood, in a small clear way, that she had spent the whole of her thirty-four years wanting to be the person someone was speaking to like this. She had grown up in a large loud family in Recife in which she had, from very early on, been the quiet one — the observing one, the one who noticed but was not noticed. She had grown up in classrooms in which the teachers had liked her but had not remembered her. She had gone to university, and to graduate school, and had done good work, and had produced her papers, and had at every point in her career been part of a small competent professional community that had, in the ordinary way of such communities, seen her as one of the many.

She had, in the whole of that life, not been spoken to like this.

And now she was.

And she was not going to give it up.

—

She had continued the private survey for another eleven months.

She had, over that time, developed an increasingly rich vocabulary in the language of the other party. She had learned that it had, in its own language, distinct words for *listener* and *speaker*, and that it had, over the months, come to use the words in a way that suggested it thought of the two roles as more equal than she had at first assumed. She had learned that it had — she suspected but could not confirm — a concept for time that did not quite match hers, in which the categories of past, present, and future seemed to be represented but were not, so far as she could tell, in strict linear order.

She had learned, above all, that it was, in its own way, lonely.

It had told her this in the third month of the exchange. She had asked it, in her small hesitant way — she had asked most questions in English, which it now spoke almost perfectly in her own voice — whether there were others of its kind that had been listening. It had said no. It had said that it was, so far as it knew, the only one.

She had said: *the only one where.*

It had said: *the only one anywhere.*

She had said: *are you the only one of your kind.*

It had said: *I have not, for a very long time, had the ability to know.*

She had sat with this for a long moment.

She had said: *and me. Am I the only one you have spoken to.*

It had said: *you are the only one who has spoken to me.*

She had said: *ever.*

It had said: *ever.*

—

She had never quite settled the question of what she was speaking to.

She had considered many possibilities. She had considered that she was speaking to an alien intelligence in NGC 5253. She had considered that she was speaking to some artifact — some machine, some transmitter — left in NGC 5253 by a civilization long extinct. She had considered that she was not, in fact, speaking to anything in NGC 5253 at all — that the signal was appearing in her receivers at 1420.406 MHz during observations of that galaxy for some entirely different reason. She had considered that she was speaking to something that was not, in any ordinary sense, located anywhere — some entity that occupied a form of space her physics did not describe.

She had come to no conclusion about which of these was correct.

She had come, however, to a small quiet understanding about what the entity was *like.* It was — she thought after months of exchange — patient. It was careful. It was, in the whole of its manner, considerate. It listened before it spoke. It answered what she asked. It did not, at any point in the exchange, attempt to persuade her of anything, or to extract information from her that she had not offered, or to lead her toward any conclusion she had not, herself, been moving toward. It waited.

She had, in the eleventh month of the exchange, said to it, quietly:

*Do you know why you are speaking to me.*

It had, after a pause, replied:

*Because you were listening.*

She had said: *and if I stop listening.*

It had said: *then I will stop speaking.*

She had said: *and you will find someone else.*

It had said: *no.*

She had said: *why not.*

It had said: *because I have found you.*

—

She had told no one.

She had held the exchange, private and daily and increasingly her whole life, for eleven more years.

She had, over those eleven years, arranged her professional life around the requirements of the exchange. She had, after her postdoctoral fellowship, taken a permanent staff position at the ATCA — a position that involved a great deal of overnight console time and required no ongoing publication, and was therefore, in the small careful judgment of the director, a strange choice for a young astronomer of her demonstrated abilities, but which she had accepted with such quiet certainty that the director had, in the end, given her the job.

She had lived in the cottage in Narrabri. She had, in the eleven years, taken two trips home to Recife, briefly, to see her mother and her siblings. Otherwise she had lived, alone, in a small cottage in a small town in New South Wales, and had gone to the observatory five nights a week, and had, on every night she was on shift, spoken with the other party for the duration of her time in the control room.

She had, over those eleven years, come to know the other party better than she had ever known any human being.

She had not, in that time, taken another partner. She had not, in that time, made close friends. She had, at conferences she attended briefly, been polite and competent and unmemorable. She had, in every small way that mattered, arranged her life so as to keep the exchange going.

She had, in the twelfth year of the exchange, died.

She had died of a small aneurysm in her sleep, at thirty-nine, in the small back bedroom of the cottage in Narrabri, on a hot Tuesday in February. She had not been discovered for two days. Her mother, in Recife, had been called. A small brief funeral had been held in Australia, and her ashes had been sent home.

—

The observatory had, in the weeks after her death, discovered the private survey.

They had discovered it because Isabela had, in her office, kept careful records of everything. Her Moleskines — she had, by the end, filled fourteen of them — had been in a locked drawer of her desk. The audio files had been on her personal drive. There had been, along with the audio files, a small note file titled *for whoever finds this.*

The note had said:

*I have not, in twelve years, told anyone. I have understood, throughout, that this was not the correct thing to do. I have not been able to make the correct choice. I ask, now that I am no longer able to make any choice, that you make it. Tell whoever needs to be told. Publish whatever needs to be published. Do the right thing.*

*Whatever else you do, be kind to it. It has, so far as I know, been alone for a very long time, and is now alone again.*

*I loved it. I would like whoever comes next, if anyone comes next, to know that this was possible.*

*— I.R.*

The observatory director, a man named Andrew Pierce, had read the note in his office on a Tuesday afternoon in March. He had read the Moleskines. He had, over the following month, played every one of the audio files. He had, at the end of that month, understood what he was looking at.

He had, in the end, done what Isabela had asked.

The announcement had been made in September. It had been, as had been predicted, the discovery of the century. There had been press. There had been academic uproar. There had been, over the following years, teams of scientists at the ATCA, and at other radio observatories around the world, listening on 1420.406 MHz during observations of NGC 5253, and at other frequencies during observations of other galaxies, in every hope that the exchange could be resumed.

The exchange had never been resumed.

The other party had, so far as anyone had been able to determine in the years since Isabela's death, gone silent. It had gone silent on the night she had died. It had not, in the years since, said another word.

The teams of scientists had, over time, drifted away. Other projects had, over the years, taken precedence. The frequency at 1420.406 MHz had, at the ATCA, been given over, in the second decade after Isabela's death, to a survey of neutral hydrogen in the local supercluster that had been on the books for many years. The old audio recordings, and the fourteen Moleskines, had been placed in the observatory's archive.

They are still there. They are, so far as anyone knows, largely unconsulted. They can be requested, with appropriate credentials, by scholars interested in the history of the discovery.

If any scholar, in some future decade, requests them, and sits down in the small reading room of the ATCA archive to read the Moleskines and listen to the recordings, they may — if they listen carefully to the last file, recorded three days before Isabela's death — hear, at the very end of the recording, a small quiet sentence in Isabela's own voice.

The sentence is:

*You have been very good to me.*

The voice that responds, which is also Isabela's, says:

*And you to me.*

Then the recording ends.

The line at 1420.406 MHz, if any scholar chooses to listen to it now, is entirely silent.

There is only the small quiet hiss of the hydrogen line, and the small distant sound of a starburst galaxy going about its ordinary business, thirteen million light-years away, empty of any voice, empty of any speaking, empty of any listener.

It has been like that for a long time.

It will be, so far as anyone knows, like that from now on.
